strengths: The problem is well motivated: predicting human responses under changing environmental feedback is relevant to cognitive modelling and adaptive interventions. Combining task-trained representations, baseline response predictions, evidence accumulation, and reinforcement learning is a potentially useful contribution.

The reported predictive improvements are promising. In Table 1, numeric-input CogReact reduces MAPE from the strongest baseline’s 0.3052 to 0.2703, approximately an 11.4% relative improvement. Leave-one-participant-out evaluation also shows improvement over pure DRL, providing some evidence of generalization across participants.

The experimental effort is substantial: 21,157 collected math-task responses, four intervention regimes, two additional application datasets, multiple input representations, and component ablations including deep-learning-plus-DDM controls. The linked code/data release and framework diagrams are valuable.
weaknesses: The central interpretation of learned trajectories as cognitive intervention effects is insufficiently supported. Appendix A.7 constructs a sigmoid-plus-Brownian trajectory from SVM predictions without establishing its correspondence to a calibrated drift-diffusion process. A terminal response-time reward cannot uniquely identify intermediate evidence accumulation: many action sequences yield the same stopping time. Actions can also compensate for baseline prediction errors, including in the no-pressure group (Figure 3a). Agreement with aggregate response-time trends therefore does not validate the claimed moment-by-moment cognitive explanation.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed temporal mechanism. The pure-DRL ablation changes the visual encoder, action scaling, and episode structure alongside removing DDM, confounding both accuracy and training-efficiency attribution. The additional DL+DDM controls are helpful, but matched sequential predictors and fitted diffusion models with stimulus-dependent parameters remain relevant comparisons. Tests with altered feedback timing or held-out intervention schedules would directly assess the stated objective. Positioning against existing RL–DDM work is also limited; conventional diffusion models can make prospective predictions.

The temporal alignment of CPC18 feedback needs clarification. Appendix A.11 describes alternative-outcome feedback as an input for predicting response time on each gambling trial. Such feedback ordinarily follows the decision. The paper must specify whether it uses preceding-trial feedback or another input available before the response; using same-trial post-response outcomes would undermine the interpretation as simulation of feedback-modulated decision time.

Statistical reporting does not establish the reliability of the gains sufficiently. Table 4 labels the empirical 2.5th and 97.5th error percentiles as a confidence interval, although these describe error dispersion rather than uncertainty in mean performance. The permutation-test sampling unit and treatment of repeated observations within participants are unspecified, and variability across training seeds is not reported. Participant-clustered paired uncertainty estimates would be more informative. Moreover, Table 8 does not establish a benefit from the risk encoder over its removal (permutation p = 0.677), weakening claims that every component is critical.

The PeerEdu evaluation requires a more appropriate metric analysis. Curiosity lies in [0,1], making MAPE unstable near zero and undefined at zero without an explicit convention. Figure 4 reports MAPE of 0.950, close to the error of 1.0 obtained by predicting zero for every strictly positive target. MAE or RMSE, explicit zero handling, and simple constant predictors are needed to assess the practical value of this extension.

Important reproduction details remain unclear despite the extensive appendix: the exact accumulation transition, sigmoid parameters, Brownian noise scale, action discount factor, and curiosity-specific dynamics are not fully specified. The paper should also state which observations train the no-pressure baseline and whether every human-data-trained stage is refitted within each evaluation split. A smaller reporting issue is the inconsistent participant count: Table 2 lists 50, Section 3 reports 44, and Appendix A.3.1 identifies 36 retained participants.
